newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler focusing on Ohio for new Jeep plant.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler focusing on Ohio for new Jeep plant.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. is more focused on sites in Ohio than in Michigan for a new factory to replace its ageing Toledo Jeep plant and hopes to announce a location decision within 90 days, Chrysler Chairman Robert Eaton said Wednesday.
Eaton, speaking to reporters at a luncheon where he was named Automotive Industries magazine's executive of the year, said Chrysler was committed to keeping the plant close to its existing workforce.
"We're more focused on Ohio" than Michigan, Eaton said.

Chrysler plans to replace the Toledo plant -- considered to be the oldest operating auto plant in the world -- with a more modern facility that industry executives expect to cost up to $1 billion. The plant, which dates back to 1910, produces Jeep Cherokee and Wrangler sport utility vehicles.

Michigan has made a pitch to Chrysler to build the new facility in Monroe County, which is in the state's far southeastern corner, just across the Ohio border from Toledo. Eaton said he has recently discussed the proposal with Michigan Gov. John Engler.

But Ohio officials have launched a massive effort to keep the plant, including plans to assemble land in the city of Toledo near the current facility for a project that would use portions of existing Chrysler buildings.
With about 5,600 workers, the Jeep plant is Toledo's largest employer.
"We're not focused on sites right now. We're focused on plant design," Eaton said.

He added that designing a plant that achieves Chrysler's capacity, efficiency and quality goals is more important than that plant's location. He declined to say whether Chrysler could better achieve its goals with a rural or urban site.

"We're committed to that workforce," he said of the Toledo workers. "We're committed to being close to where they are now so they don't have to drive a long way. We're committed to a modern plant that will carry us maybe not as long as the last one did, but into the middle of the next century."
Under its contract with the United Auto Workers, Chrysler cannot ask workers to commute more than 50 miles from their current plant location.
